name: Seed grinding at Cuddie Springs, New South Wales
summary: People at Cuddie Springs in New South Wales were grinding plant food on sandstone grindstones more than 30,000 years ago, with wear and starch pointing to flour making.
description: A fragment from the rim of a sandstone grindstone found at the Cuddie Springs archaeological site, on Wailwan Country in New South Wales, is over 30,000 years old. According to the Australian Museum, analysis of its use-wear and starch residue supports the use of grindstones to make flour. A 2022 study reports still older seed-grinding stones at Madjedbebe in northern Australia, so Cuddie Springs is not the earliest case in Australia.

impact.note: Grinding made hard plant foods usable, an improvement to gathering shown here for one inland community and its region, with no later development shown to descend from this site.

date.label: over 30,000 years ago (before c. 28,050 BCE)
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: A grindstone fragment from the Cuddie Springs archaeological site in New South Wales shows food preparation dating back over 30,000 years (before about 28,050 BCE).

evidence.supports: found in the Cuddie Springs archaeological site, on Wailwan Country, demonstrates the longevity of food preparation dating back over 30,000 years

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The museum page speaks of food preparation and flour. That the plant food was seed rests on Fullagar and Field (1997, Antiquity), of which only the title page could be opened (it gives no date), and on Hayes et al. 2022, who count Cuddie Springs among Pleistocene seed-grinding examples; the radiocarbon range should be taken from the 1997 paper.
Hayes et al. (2022, Scientific Reports) report seed-grinding stones at Madjedbebe from its Phase 2 (68,700–50,400 years ago); that find deserves its own sourced event or record.
The coordinates need checking against a gazetteer.

research.note: No source says how the practice arose here; a 2022 study of Madjedbebe describes its own stones as the earliest known seed-grinding implements in Australia, older than the Cuddie Springs examples, and cites older seed grinding in Africa.
